text:
An approval screen can reassure without proving enough.

CERT-In reports an AI-assisted campaign targeting Indian financial entities through their payment interfaces. Its earlier advisory describes stolen credentials enabling direct payment requests that bypass application checks.

That distinction is where I think leaders need to spend time. A screen can show that someone approved a payment. It does not, by itself, establish that the system moving the money requires that approval.

I would be careful about assuming every payment system has this weakness. But I would be equally careful about accepting a reassuring display as evidence that the final transfer is controlled.

My practical takeaway: ask the business and technology owners to trace one approved payment together, from the decision to the transfer. Have them show what prevents the final step from sending a different amount, paying a different recipient, or proceeding without approval.

The confidence worth having comes from seeing that the permission granted is the permission enforced when money moves.
